Any complex number [MATH: z] can be written in polar form as

Content:

where

Content:
[MATH: r = |z|, \qquad \theta = \arg(z).]

Content:
Recall that the [MATH: n]th roots of [MATH: z] are given by

Content:

sections.normalized_html:
Any nonzero complex number [MATH: z] has exactly [MATH: n] distinct [MATH: n]th roots. Using de Moivre's theorem, we can write down these roots as

[MATH: z_{k}^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{r}\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{\theta+2\pi{k}}{n}\right)+\textrm{i}\sin\left(\dfrac{\theta+2\pi{k}}{n}\right)\right],]

where

[MATH: r = |z|, \qquad \theta = \arg(z), \qquad k=0, 1, 2,..., n-1.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: r=1, \qquad \theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \qquad n=6.]

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain

[MATH: z_{k}^{1/6}|= root(1, 6)[\cos (((3π)/(2) + 2πk)/(6)) + \textrm{i}\sin (((3π)/(2) + 2πk)/(6))]; = \cos ((π)/(4) + π 3 ⋅ k) + \textrm{i}\sin ((π)/(4) + π 3 ⋅ k).]

Therefore, [MATH: a={\color{blue}4}] and [MATH: b={\color{red}\dfrac{\pi}{3}}.]

Any nonzero complex number [MATH: z] has exactly [MATH: n] distinct [MATH: n]th roots. Using de Moivre's theorem, we can write down these roots as

where

[MATH: r = |z|, \qquad \theta = \arg(z), \qquad k=0, 1, 2,..., n-1.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: r=1, \qquad \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \qquad n=4.]

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain
